Automated detection of transitional vertebral anatomy for wrong-level spine surgery prevention: (A) a segmenter-agnostic classifier that flags transitional vertebrae on preoperative CT, and (B) a neural network that names vertebral levels from a single intraoperative C-arm exposure without registration to a preoperative scan

Provide a narrative description of the invention/technology/innovation/idea. What is novel or unexpected? Please provide sufficient technical detail to convey a clear understanding to the extent known at the time of disclosure.

Problem. Wrong-level spine surgery is a never event whose largest anatomic driver is a transitional vertebra (a sixth lumbar vertebra, a thirteenth thoracic vertebra, or a fifth lumbar vertebra fused to the sacrum; 5-35 % of people). Planning is done on lumbar-only CT without a count from C2, and intraoperative confirmation is counting vertebral bodies on fluoroscopy; both fail on transitional spines, and registration-based aids (LevelCheck-type systems) project the labels of the preoperative read and inherit its counting error. Current CT segmenters (TotalSegmentator, SPINEPS) shift the lumbar labels one level on such spines without warning.

Part A -- preoperative CT flag (near-term product). A classifier that takes the output of ANY CT segmenter, discards the segmenter's level names, and computes name-free per-vertebra features (rib presence traced in the CT image, rib-free body count above the sacral plateau, transverse-process-to-sacral-ala contact area, disc and end-plate geometry, iliac crest line), then flags the transitional phenotype (L6, sacralised L5 by Castellvi grade, T13, lumbar rib, four lumbar) with a plain-language reason, an abstention when the junction is outside the field of view, and an 'unusual spine' score.

Part B -- intraoperative level naming. A convolutional-recurrent network reads a single C-arm exposure, detects the vertebral bodies and the sacrum, and names each level from LOCAL MORPHOLOGY rather than from a count, so a transitional vertebra is recognised as what it is; the classifier is coupled with a count from the detected sacrum through a set of candidate vertebral sequences ('alphabets', ordinary and transitional) and abstains visibly when they disagree. No registration, fiducials or navigation hardware. It is trained on digitally reconstructed radiographs rendered from labelled CT through per-device image-formation models (fitted physics parameters per C-arm model; free geometric labels by projection, including the bicoxofemoral point) plus few real frames per device. Measured: on a C-arm never seen in training it named 96.4 % of detected lateral vertebrae zero-shot (595 of 617) and 97.4 % after case-grouped fine-tuning; in its feature space a sixth lumbar vertebra separates from the fifth more than the fifth from the fourth (silhouette 0.35 vs 0.23).

Novel or unexpected: level identity learned from local morphology instead of counting or registration; the alphabet coupling with visible abstention; per-device image-formation models that let one network serve several C-arms from renders with few real frames; a segmenter-agnostic, name-free CT flag. Unexpected: naming accuracy on an unseen C-arm reached its plateau before any real frame of that device was used for training -- the limit is coverage of acquisition geometry, not the number of real images.
Does the invention/technology/innovation/idea involve a new process or method, composition of matter or device, software or combination?

Combination: new processes/methods (name-free transitional-phenotype classification from segmentations; level naming from local morphology coupled with a count and abstention; render-based per-device training) embodied in software (trained neural-network weights, training and inference code, per-device image-formation parameters).
Does the invention/technology/innovation/idea involve a new use, or an improvement of an existing product or process?

Improvement of existing processes: preoperative CT planning (a flag on the planning scan) and intraoperative fluoroscopic level confirmation. New use of any vendor's CT segmenter output as the input of a transitional-anatomy flag.
Describe the product/services that are expected from the development of the invention/technology/innovation/idea.

(A) Software as a medical device that flags suspected transitional anatomy on preoperative CT and notifies the reader -- radiology/PACS workflow, Class II 510(k) anticipated (product codes QIH/MYN), the near-term product. (B) Intraoperative level confirmation on the C-arm exposure -- decision support beside the surgeon's count, integrated with C-arm consoles or navigation platforms (harder regulatory path; later). (C) Licensable assets: per-device image-formation parameters, the evaluation protocol and reference standard, trained weights retrained on commercially licensed data.

What is the stage of development of the invention/technology/innovation/idea? E.g., still in conceptual/idea stage, functioning prototype, fully developed product? Please explain.

Functioning research prototypes: trained weights exist for Part B and are evaluated on public intraoperative datasets (C-ArmLSpine C-arm frames with cone-beam CT truth; COBRA2026 kV frames) and on rendered CT; Part A's feature extractor runs on 3,500 CT-segmenter pairs and its classifier is in training; a manuscript on Part B is in preparation; no prospective or clinical evaluation; no regulatory submission. The prototypes are trained on non-commercially licensed research data (see Resources); a commercial model must be rebuilt from commercially licensed data.
What is the market opportunity for the invention/technology/innovation/idea? Please describe the market, potential customers, and unmet need or problem/solution it addresses.

Every spine operation confirms its level under fluoroscopy and is planned on CT or MRI; over one million spine procedures are performed each year in the United States. Wrong-level surgery is a reportable never event (half of responding spine surgeons report having performed one; registry rate about 0.1 %, higher in the thoracic spine), and transitional vertebrae (5-35 % prevalence) are its largest anatomic cause. Customers: radiology groups and PACS/AI platform vendors (Part A); hospitals and ambulatory surgery centres, C-arm and navigation manufacturers (Part B). Unmet need: a check that does not fail on exactly the anatomy that causes the error, works on the limited fields of view actually acquired, and needs no registered preoperative scan.
How is the need currently being met and/or any known alternative solutions or competitive products? Describe the commercial market in which the invention/technology/innovation/idea would compete.

Manual counting on fluoroscopy with a marker and a check film; intraoperative navigation (registration of the preoperative CT/CBCT to the patient; hardware, fiducials, time); LevelCheck-type research systems (Johns Hopkins) that register the preoperative scan and project its labels -- accurate on ordinary spines, dependent on the planning read; CT segmenters and vendor spine-labelling tools (TotalSegmentator/3D Slicer, MSKai-type products) that mislabel transitional spines by one level without warning. No product today flags a transitional vertebra on the planning CT or names one from a single C-arm exposure.

What advantages does the invention/technology/innovation/idea possess over existing or emerging technologies?

Built for the transitional anatomy on which counting, registration and current segmenters fail; segmenter-agnostic and name-free, so it audits any vendor's output without retraining it; registration-free intraoperative naming from one exposure with visible abstention; one network serves several C-arm models through per-device image-formation parameters, so adapting to a new device needs few real frames; every call carries a plain-language reason.
